name: Theories
question: Does the paper build on or contribute to this theory (not merely mention it)?

labels.name: resource-based view
labels.definition: Competitive advantage from valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable resources (Barney, Wernerfelt).

labels.name: dynamic capabilities
labels.definition: The capacity to sense, seize and reconfigure resources as environments change (Teece, Eisenhardt and Martin).

labels.name: resource orchestration
labels.definition: How managers structure, bundle and leverage resources (Sirmon, Hitt).

labels.name: institutional theory
labels.definition: Organizations conform to institutional pressures for legitimacy: coercive, mimetic, normative isomorphism.

labels.name: transaction cost economics
labels.definition: Governance choices (make or buy, contracts) minimize transaction costs given asset specificity and uncertainty (Williamson).

labels.name: agency theory
labels.definition: Principal–agent relationships, goal conflict, information asymmetry and incentive alignment.

labels.name: stakeholder theory
labels.definition: Firms create value for, and are accountable to, multiple stakeholders beyond shareholders (Freeman).

labels.name: contingency theory
labels.definition: No best way to organize: performance depends on the fit between structure or strategy and context.

labels.name: network theory
labels.definition: Social or inter-organizational networks, ties, structural holes and embeddedness shape outcomes.

labels.name: attention-based view
labels.definition: Firm behavior follows from how decision-makers' attention is focused and distributed (Ocasio).

labels.name: behavioral theory of the firm
labels.definition: Bounded rationality, aspirations, search and organizational learning (Cyert and March).

labels.name: absorptive capacity
labels.definition: A firm's ability to recognize, assimilate and apply external knowledge (Cohen and Levinthal; Zahra and George).

labels.name: resource dependence theory
labels.definition: Organizations depend on external resources; power and dependence shape their strategies and ties (Pfeffer and Salancik).

labels.name: conservation of resources theory
labels.definition: People and organizations strive to gain, protect and rebuild resources; loss spirals under stress (Hobfoll).

labels.name: paradox theory
labels.definition: Persistent contradictory yet interrelated demands (organizational tensions) and how they are navigated (Smith and Lewis).

labels.name: sensemaking
labels.definition: How people notice, interpret and enact ambiguous situations, often retrospectively, to act (Weick).

labels.name: bricolage
labels.definition: Making do with the resources at hand, recombining them for new purposes (Lévi-Strauss; Baker and Nelson).

labels.name: practice theory
labels.definition: Social life as practices: routinized doings and sayings, with their materials, meanings and competences (Schatzki, Reckwitz, Giddens).

labels.name: process theory
labels.definition: Phenomena explained as unfolding sequences of events and becoming over time, not variance between variables (Langley, Van de Ven).

labels.name: actor-network theory
labels.definition: Human and non-human actors assembled through translation into networks; agency is relational (Latour, Callon, Law).

labels.name: assemblage theory
labels.definition: Wholes as contingent assemblages of heterogeneous parts whose relations, not essences, define them (Deleuze and Guattari, DeLanda).

labels.name: sociomateriality
labels.definition: The social and the material are constitutively entangled in organizational practice (Orlikowski, Scott).

labels.name: socio-technical systems
labels.definition: Work systems designed by jointly optimizing their social and technical subsystems (Trist, Emery).

labels.name: multi-level perspective
labels.definition: Socio-technical transitions through interactions of niches, regimes and the landscape (Geels).

labels.name: path dependence
labels.definition: Early events and increasing returns lock trajectories in; history constrains later choices (David, Arthur, Sydow).

labels.name: punctuated equilibrium
labels.definition: Long periods of stability broken by short bursts of fundamental change (Gersick, Tushman and Romanelli).

labels.name: coevolution
labels.definition: Organizations and their environments, or populations of them, evolve jointly and shape each other (Lewin and Volberda).

labels.name: complex adaptive systems
labels.definition: Systems of interacting agents that self-organize and adapt; emergence and nonlinearity (Holland; Choi, Dooley and Rungtusanatham).

labels.name: game theory
labels.definition: Strategic interaction between rational players whose payoffs depend on each other's choices.

labels.name: ecosystems
labels.definition: Business, innovation or platform ecosystems: interdependent actors co-creating value around a focal offer (Adner, Jacobides).

labels.name: platform theory
labels.definition: Multi-sided platforms, network effects and the governance of complementors (Parker and Van Alstyne, Gawer).

labels.name: service-dominant logic
labels.definition: Value is co-created by actors exchanging service; goods are vehicles for service (Vargo and Lusch).

labels.name: public service logic
labels.definition: Public services as co-produced with users, value created in use rather than delivered (Osborne).

labels.name: critical theory
labels.definition: Critique of power, domination and taken-for-granted assumptions in organizations and society (Frankfurt School, critical management studies).

labels.name: cliodynamics
labels.definition: Mathematical and quantitative models of long-run historical dynamics, cycles and societal instability (Turchin).

labels.name: integral theory
labels.definition: An all-quadrant, all-level framework integrating individual and collective, interior and exterior perspectives (Wilber).
